Matous Konecny
mat'oush ko'nech-ne
n. (Matous Konecny, 1569–1622, bishop of the Unity of the Brethren at Mlada Boleslav)
Czech Matous from Hebrew Mattithyah, gift of the LORD; Konecny, final, last, a Czech surname.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Matous Konecny was a bishop of the Unity of the Brethren at Mlada Boleslav and the author of practical Czech divinity for ordinary households, including a long work on the duties of the Christian estates — magistrates, ministers, parents, children, masters, servants. He died in 1622, in the first wave of the Bohemian proscription, and before the end he had his library and papers walled up in the Brethren house at Mlada Boleslav. They were found in 2006, four centuries later: hundreds of books and letters bricked into a cavity by men who expected to come back. The dictionary ends this batch there deliberately. A church being destroyed hid its books in a wall, and the men who laid the bricks were wrong about returning and right about the books. Konecny's own subject was the ordinary Christian calling — how a father, a servant or a magistrate serves God in the place he is set — and that is what survived the wall.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines calling as one's usual occupation or employment, and immure as to shut up within walls.

expand to see more

CALL'ING, n. A proper or usual occupation or employment; the divine summons to a station in life.

IMMU'RE, v.t. To wall in; to enclose within walls; to shut up; to confine.

ES'TATE, n. Condition or circumstances of any person or thing; a rank or order in a commonwealth.

LI'BRARY, n. A collection of books belonging to a private person or to a public institution.

Key Scripture

1Co 7:24 — "Brethren, let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God."

Eph 6:5 — "Servants, be obedient to them that are your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, in singleness of your heart, as unto Christ;"

Col 3:23 — "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;"

Jer 32:14 — "Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Take these evidences, this evidence of the purchase, both which is sealed, and this evidence which is open; and put them in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days."

Modern Corruption

He wrote on the ordinary Christian callings, and had the Brethren library bricked into a wall in 1622.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern separation of the spiritual life from the ordinary calling, so that a servant, a father or a town councillor looks for his religion in what he does after work. Konecny wrote a whole volume on the opposite: the duties of each estate, performed as service to Christ, are the Christian life for most Christians most of the time.

The principle to recover is that God assigns a station and is served in it. “Brethren, let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God” (1Co 7:24). Even bondservice is turned into worship: “And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23). And the hiding of the books has a biblical shape, for Jeremiah too was told to seal the deeds of a doomed country and store them against a future he would not see: “and put them in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days” (Jer 32:14).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek klesis (G2821), a calling, a vocation; Hebrew kli (H3627), a vessel, an instrument.

Greek klesis (G2821) — a calling, an invitation, a vocation; 1 Corinthians 7:24.

Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, to remain, to continue; 1 Corinthians 7:24.

Greek psuche (G5590) — the soul; and so heartily, from the soul; Colossians 3:23.

Hebrew kli (H3627) — a vessel, an implement; Jeremiah 32:14.

Hebrew cheres (H2789) — earthenware, a potsherd; Jeremiah 32:14.

Usage

"“let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God” (1Co 7:24) — a volume on the Christian estates."

"“do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23) — written for households, not for schools."

"“that they may continue many days” (Jer 32:14) — a library bricked up in 1622 and found in 2006."
